title.en: Arthur of Britain Steals Finn's Hounds
title.zh: 不列顛之亞瑟竊取芬恩獵犬

region.en: Inver Mara Gamiach, coast of Britain
region.zh: 不列顛海岸卡拉馬基河口

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Arthur son of the King of Britain takes service with Finn, then runs off across the sea with the three hounds Bran, Sceolan and Adhnuall. Finn reads the theft in his pale-gold basin of water and sends nine champions after them; Goll spares Arthur's life, and the captive prince bonds with Finn and follows him till he dies. From the bay mare Goll seized on the way descends all the horses of the Fianna; and Finn's hounds had been lost before — to a witch whose enchanted breath shut three times fifty of them in the Mound of the Hounds.
summary.zh: 不列顛王子亞瑟曾投效芬恩，卻攜三犬布蘭、斯克奧蘭、艾德努爾渡海而逃。芬恩於淡金水盆中窺知竊案，遣九位英雄追討；戈爾饒亞瑟一命，被俘王子向芬恩立誓終身相隨。途中戈爾奪得的母馬，其後代即菲亞納全部馬匹；此外芬恩之犬曾被女巫以魔息關入犬冢三次五十隻，永不再出。

sensitivity.note: This Arthur is a Fenian-cycle British prince, not the Arthur of the romances — a useful cross-cycle witness. Scrying in a basin of pale gold parallels Manannan's tokens; the witch's hound-mound (Duma na nCon) is a dindsenchas-style etiology. Pin symbolic on the British coast.

passages.text: Arthur, son of the King of Britain, came one time to take service with Finn, and three times nine men along with him. And while Arthur was there he took notice of three of Finn's hounds, Bran, and Sceolan and Adhnuall, and he made a plan to go away across the sea, himself and his three nines, bringing those three hounds along with him. So he did that, and the place where they landed was Inver Mara Gamiach on the coast of Britain, and they went to the mountain of Lodan, son of Lir, to hunt on it. As to the Fianna, after their hunting was done they gathered together on the hill, and all Finn's hounds were counted — three hundred full-grown hounds he had and two hundred whelps, and to be counting them was like counting the branches on a tree. On this day Bran and Sceolan and Adhnuall were missing. Then Finn sent for a long-shaped basin of pale gold, and water in it, and he put his face in the water, and his hand over his face, and it was showed him what had happened, and he said: "The King of Britain's son has brought away the hound. And let nine men be chosen out to follow after them."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: Arthur of Britain and his people were sitting on a hunting mound just at that time, and the nine men of the Fianna made an attack on them and killed all of them but Arthur, that Goll, son of Morna, put his two arms about and saved from death. Then they turned to go back to Ireland, bringing Arthur with them, and the three hounds; and as they were going, Goll saw a dark-grey horse and a bay mare that was not easy to get hold of, and he gave them into Oisin's hand, and he gave them on to Diarmuid. Arthur made bonds with Finn, and was his follower till he died. And as to the mare, she bred eight times, at every birth eight foals, and it is of that seed came all the horses of the fair Fianna of the Gael, for they had used no horses up to that time. And that was not the only time Finn was robbed of some of his hounds, for a woman-Druid of the Tuatha de Danaan set her love on Finn, and he said, so long as there was another woman to be found in the world, he would not marry a witch; and one time three times fifty of Finn's hounds passed by the hill where she was, and she breathed on the hounds and shut them up in the hill, and they never came out again, and the place got the name of Duma na Conn, the Mound of the Hounds.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Hags and the Hanks of Yarn at Ceiscoran
title.zh: 凱斯克蘭的三巫與紗束

region.en: Cave of Ceiscoran, Slieve League, Co. Donegal, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭多尼戈爾郡凱斯克蘭洞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: To avenge Finn's great hunting, Conaran of the Tuatha de Danaan sends his three hag daughters to the mouth of a cave with enchanted hanks of yarn reeled on crooked holly-sticks. Champion after champion passes the hanks and collapses into weakness, to be bound and dragged into the cave — until Goll of Morna, the Flame of Battle, cuts two hags through with one blow, wrestles the oldest down, and spares her when she puts her body under the protection of his bravery and restores every man of the Fianna.
summary.zh: 為報復芬恩的大狩獵，神族科納蘭派三名巫婆女兒到洞穴口，以彎曲冬青杖上的魔紗束作祟。一個個英雄經過紗束便氣力盡失，被捆入洞中——直到戰火之焰戈爾一劍穿透兩巫，摔倒最年長者；她以身家性命托庇於他的勇武而得赦，將菲亞納眾人全數釋放。

sensitivity.note: The yarn-hank binding spell is a distinct Irish binding-magic motif (compare the binding of battles in Ulster tradition); the hag-battle inverts the fairy-mistress pattern. Pin symbolic at the traditional cave site.

passages.text: Finn called for a great hunt one time on the plains of Magh Chonaill and in the forest parts of Cairbre of the Nuts, and he himself went up to the top of Ceiscoran, and his two dogs Bran and Sceolan with him. Conaran, son of Imidd, of the Tuatha de Danaan, had the sway in Ceiscoran at that time, and when he heard the shouting and the cry of the hounds all around, he bade his three daughters that had a great share of enchantments to do vengeance on Finn for his hunting. The three women went to the opening of a cave that was in the hills, and there they sat down together, and put three strong enchanted hanks of yarn on crooked holly-sticks, and began to reel them off outside the cave. They were not long there till Finn and Conan came towards them, and saw the three ugly old hags at their work, their coarse hair tossed, their eyes red and bleary, their teeth sharp and crooked, their arms very long, their nails like the tips of cows' horns, and the three spindles in their hands. Finn and Conan passed through the hanks of yarn to get a better look at the hags, and no sooner had they done that than a deadly trembling came on them and a weakness, and the bold hags took hold of them and put them in tight bonds.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Two other men of the Fianna came up then, and the sons of Menhann along with them, and their strength went from them in the same way; and in the end the whole number of them, gentle and simple, were put in bonds by the hags and brought into the cave, while a great outcry of hounds calling for their masters began at the mouth of the cave. Then they saw coming towards them a very tall man that was Goll, son of Morna, the Flame of Battle, and the three hags went to meet him and fought a hard battle with him. Great anger came on Goll, and he raised up his sword, and with one blow he cut the two that were nearest him through and through; and the oldest of the three women wound her arms about him, and they wrestled together till Goll gave her a great twist and threw her on the ground, and tied her fast with the straps of a shield. But the hag said: "O champion that was never worsted, I put my body and my life under the protection of your bravery. And it is better for you to get Finn and the Fianna safe and whole than to have my blood." With that Goll set her free, and she took off the fastenings, first from Fergus of the True Lips and the other learned men of the Fianna, and after that from Finn and Oisin and the twenty-nine sons of Morna and all the rest, and Fergus made great praises of Goll for all he had done.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Donn son of Midhir and the Hidden House under the Snow
title.zh: 米德之子東恩與雪下隱宅

region.en: Slieve-nam-Ban (Mountain of the Women), Co. Tipperary, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭蒂珀雷里郡女人山

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: A beautiful fawn lures Finn and six men across Ireland to Slieve-nam-Ban and vanishes into the earth as heavy snow falls; Caoilte finds a lighted house of the Sidhe, and Donn son of Midhir tells how he and twenty-eight brothers refused hostages to Bodb Dearg, were threatened with the walling-up of their dwelling, and fight three battles a year with the Men of Dea. Finn and the Fianna stand with them at fall of night and slaughter ten hundred ten score and ten, until Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh ends the feud with a wall of fire and a wall of water.
summary.zh: 一頭美麗母鹿引芬恩與六人穿越愛爾蘭至女人山，在大雪中遁入地下。卡爾特尋得燈火通明的仙族宅邸；米德之子東恩講述：因拒絕向波德·迪爾格獻人質，兄弟二十九人遭封居之威脅，每年與神族交戰三次。芬恩與菲亞納於夜幕時分馳援，斬敵一千二百一十，直到利爾以火牆與水牆結束世仇。

sensitivity.note: The hidden house (bruiden) under a fairy hill is a hall-myth of the Fenian-Sidhe interface; hostage-refusal and the walling-up threat mirror the Bodb Dearg kingship records. The fawn-lure repeats the Sadbh pattern — in this cycle deer of the Sidhe are recurrent envoys. Pin is the named Slieve-na-mBan.

passages.text: One time the Fianna were at their hunting at the island of Toraig to the north of Ireland, and they roused a fawn that was very wild and beautiful, and Finn and six of his men followed after it through the whole country, till they came to Slieve-nam-Ban. And there the fawn put down its head and vanished into the earth. A heavy snow began to fall then that bent down the tops of the trees, and the courage and the strength went from the Fianna, and Finn said to Caoilte: "Is there any place we can find shelter to-night?" Caoilte made himself supple and went over the elbow of the hill southward, and he saw a house full of light, with cups and horns and bowls of different sorts in it, and he knew it to be a house of the Sidhe, and he went in. On the one side he saw eight-and-twenty armed men, each of them having a well-shaped woman beside him; and on the other side six nice young girls, yellow-haired; and in the middle a young girl with a harp, playing and singing, and they were all making mirth around her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Those eight-and-twenty armed men," said the tall man, "had the one father and mother with myself; we are the sons of Midhir of the Yellow Hair, and our mother is Fionnchaem, the fair beautiful daughter of the King of the Sidhe of Monaid in the east. At one time the Tuatha de Danaan gave the kingship to Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, and he began to ask hostages of myself and of my brothers; but we said that till all the rest of the Men of Dea had given them, we would not give them. Bodb Dearg said then to our father: 'Unless you will put away your sons, we will wall up your dwelling-place on you.' So the eight-and-twenty brothers of us came out to look for a place for ourselves, and we are here ever since, and my own name is Donn, son of Midhir. The Men of Dea come three times in every year to give battle to us on the green outside." Finn and the Fianna stood with them at the fall of night, for that was the hour the Men of Dea chose to do them the most harm, and from the covering time of evening to the edge of the morning they fought the battle, and the loss of the Tuatha de Danaan was no less a number than ten hundred ten score and ten men. Then Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh, the oldest of them, gave his advice: let every one carry away his dead, "and as for us that stop here, let a wall of fire be made about us on the one side, and a wall of water on the other side."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: Caoilte Carries Off the Physician Luibra
title.zh: 卡爾特擄走醫師盧伊布拉

region.en: Ford of the Slaine, plain of Leinster, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭倫斯特平原斯拉因淺灘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: A year of three battles under the hill leaves Conn son of Midhir dead and two Fianna near death, their wounds held off their bodies with bent hazel sticks. Donn knows only one physician can cure them — the Tuatha de Danaan's own, who gathers healing herbs at dawn while the dew is on them. "Living or dead, I will bring him with me," says Caoilte, and under a Druid mist he and two sons of Midhir carry the physician off; the cure is promised under threat of the head, and within nine days the men are sound again.
summary.zh: 一年三戰令米德之子康恩陣亡，兩名菲亞納戰士瀕死，傷處須以彎榛杖撐開衣物。東恩言唯有神族醫師可治——他每日黎明趁露采藥。「生死不論，我必帶他回來」，卡爾特與米德二子在德魯伊霧中將醫師擄走；以人頭為質索得醫術，九日之內傷者痊癒。

sensitivity.note: The dawn-dew herb gathering and nine-day cure reproduce Asclepieion-style healing logic in the Fenian frame; the forced conscription of the enemy's physician is a raid-law motif (fleet hostage-taking in Irish law). Tagged 'resurrection' for the wound-restoring function as in the Conn Crither record.

passages.text: Conn, son of Midhir, was killed in one of the battles; and as to the Fianna, there were so many wounds on them that the clothing was held off from their bodies with bent hazel sticks, and they lying in their beds, and two of them were like to die. "Good Donn," said Finn, "have you knowledge of any physician that can cure our men?" "I only know one physician could do that," said Donn; "a physician the Tuatha de Danaan have with them. And unless a wounded man has the marrow of his back cut through, he will get relief from that physician, the way he will be sound at the end of nine days." "How can we bring that man here, for those he is with are no good friends to us?" "He goes out every morning at break of day to gather healing herbs while the dew is on them." "Find some one, Donn," said Caoilte, "that will show me that physician, and, living or dead, I will bring him with me."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Aedh and Flann, two of the sons of Midhir, rose up and went on before Caoilte to a green lawn with the dew on it, and there they saw a strong young man armed and having a cloak of the wool of the seven sheep of the Land of Promise, full of herbs of healing he was after gathering for the Men of Dea that were wounded in the battle. They ran at him together, and Caoilte took him by the shoulders, and they brought him away with them to the ford of the Slaine in the great plain of Leinster, and a Druid mist rose up about them that they could not be seen. Finn and Donn gave a great welcome to Luibra, the physician, and showed him their two comrades. "Those men can be cured if I get a good reward." "It will take nine days," said Luibra. "It is a good reward you will get, and this is what it is, your own life to be left to you; but if these young men are not healed, it is my own hand will strike off your head." And within nine days the physician had done a cure on them, and they were as well and as sound as before.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Feast of Teamhair: Finn Given Up for Lost
title.zh: 塔拉盛宴：芬恩被認定失踪

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: A year after Finn vanished under the hill, the High King opens the Feast of Teamhair and offers Goll the hunting-rights of Ireland; Goll refuses Finn's place until three years and all hope are gone. Seventeen queens of Finn's household are given safe sunny houses, Berngal keeps the spear and hound's collar Finn left him at their parting, and the Druid Cithruadh — whose every foretelling had come true — announces: before the feast is over you will see the Leader of the Fianna drinking at it.
summary.zh: 芬恩隱入仙丘一年後，至高王設塔拉盛宴，將愛爾蘭獵權許予戈爾；戈爾拒絕頂替——除非三年已過、眾人絕望。芬恩家室十七位夫人各獲安全宅邸；伯恩加爾珍藏分手時芬恩所贈長矛與犬項圈；德魯伊西斯魯——其預言從未落空——宣佈：盛宴未散，你們將見菲亞納之首於此舉杯。

sensitivity.note: The disappearance-and-search assembly is the fixed narrative hinge between Fenian episodes (a year and a quarter being the legal term of absence in Irish tradition). Cithruadh's oracle functions as the tale's plot-charm; retained as divination motif.

passages.text: It was after that time the High King sent a messenger to bring the Fianna to the Feast of Teamhair, and they all gathered to it, men and women, boys and heroes and musicians. Goll, son of Morna, was sitting at the feast beside the king. "It is a great loss you have had, Fianna of Ireland, losing your lord and your leader, Finn, son of Cumhal." "It is a great loss indeed," said Goll. "There has no greater loss fallen on Ireland since the loss of Lugh, son of Ethne. What orders will you give to the Fianna now, king?" "To yourself, Goll, I will give the right of hunting over all Ireland till we know if the loss of Finn is lasting." "I will not take Finn's place," said Goll, "till he has been wanting to us through the length of three years, and till no person in Ireland has any hope of seeing him again."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the king stood up, a smooth drinking-horn in his hand: "It would be a good thing, men of Ireland, if any one among you could get us news of Finn in hills or in secret places, or in rivers or invers, or in any house of the Sidhe in Ireland or in Alban." With that Berngal, the cow-owner from the borders of Slieve Fuad, said: "The day Finn came out from the north, following after a deer of the Sidhe, he put a sharp spear having a shining head in my hand, and a hound's collar along with it, and he bade me to keep them till he would meet me again in the same place." The High King called then to Cithruadh, the Druid, and he said: "It is much riches and many treasures Finn gave you, and tell us now is he living or is he dead?" "He is living," said Cithruadh; "but as to where he is, I will give no news of that, for he himself would not like me to give news of it." There was great joy among them, for everything Cithruadh had ever foretold had come true. "Tell us when will he come back?" "Before the Feast of Teamhair is over," said the Druid, "you will see the Leader of the Fianna drinking at it." And on the last day of the Feast of Teamhair they came back to their people again, and from that time out the Fianna of Ireland had not more dealings with the people living in houses than they had with the People of the Gods of Dana.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. III; not verbatim.
